en: In this regard, we shall first set forth the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) in order to establish that the entire universe proceeds under the control of a single being.

Regarding this, the Mīmāṃsakas say: "This person endowed with the power to perceive all objects does not deserve to be accepted, because he lies beyond the scope of any possible means of valid cognition that could establish him, and because there are clear and manifold subverting arguments against him.
For instance, would his proof be perception or something else?"
Is perception also either worldly (*laukika*) or technical (*yaugika*)?
First of all, it is not the worldly [perception] here that is established as having a restricted scope regarding its own object;
for by means of that [worldly perception], the proof of "all objects" or of the knowledge thereof and so forth is unestablished.

For one who intends to convey [the Buddha] as being endowed with the power to perceive all objects, every object—whether separated by space, time, or intrinsic nature—must be brought within the range of both perception and that power.

Now, it is impossible for ordinary perception, which functions only toward a limited number of objects suitable for contact with the currently existing sense faculties, to possess such an infinite majesty as to be a ground for possibility; how, then, could we consider it a means of proof in this case?
Nor is the perception of a yogin a proof for this [self], because, insofar as it is a form of perception, that too has only what is presently existing as its object;
it does not have the past and so forth as its object, just like a mental intuition (*pratibhā*) and the like. (Yiś 3)
Now, is that consciousness of the yogin sensory (aindriyaka) or not?
If it is sensory, does it arise from the external sense organs or from the internal organ (manas)?
It is well known in the world that the external sense organs generate cognitions of their respective objects only when accompanied by contact with their own specific objects.
Therefore, there is no undesirable consequence of the senses, such as the sense of taste, perceiving all objects—whether unarisen, past, or obstructed.
Nor is contact possible with non-existent things, such as those that are unarisen and so forth; for contact requires a locus, and in the absence of a locus, it cannot occur.
Therefore, contact with the object is required.
In the absence of such auxiliary factors, how could the sense organs be capable of directly perceiving objects that are past or otherwise remote?
And it is a fact that whatever serves as an auxiliary for something is necessary for the production of its effect.
In the absence of those [auxiliaries], that [cause] does not produce it;

for example, a seed which produces the effect of a sprout when assisted by earth and water does not produce a sprout in the absence of earth and so forth. Since the external sense-faculties produce cognition only when assisted by contact with an object (*arthasannikarṣa*), they too do not produce cognition regarding an object that is past or future. Therefore, the perception produced by them does not possess the aforementioned restriction regarding its object.
It does not transcend [the senses], nor is there the possibility of an intermediate organ,
because [the self] possesses sovereignty over its own internal [faculties] regarding pleasure and so forth, which are indeed the internal objects of experience.
For if one were to admit that the mind acts without restraint toward external objects, then the eyes and other sense organs would be rendered useless;
consequently, someone might as well be blind or deaf.
Furthermore, there is a point of contention here: the mind does not operate within the sphere of external perception independently of the external sense organs.
In that case, because it functions in dependence upon that [other factor]: whatever functions here in dependence upon something else does not operate there independently of it,
just as the eye, which functions in dependence upon light, does not operate with respect to its own object in total darkness.

Nor is it possible that the senses— having attained excellence through the power of perfected herbs, mantras, asceticism, and meditative absorption— should ever abandon the restriction regarding their respective objects;
for those [means] have as their sole fruit the manifestation of innate capacities,
and such capacity is restricted by its very nature.

Indeed, even the auditory organ, despite being refined by the application of hundreds of well-prepared medicines, is not capable of perceiving the manifestation of color or taste. Furthermore, there exists an excellence of proficiency in the external and internal instruments under discussion— which are the subject of dispute— that does not overstep its limits,
because it is a preeminent state of the sense organs.
Cognition produced by the senses, like that which perceives an excellence [of an object] currently being seen, does not take the past and so forth as its object;

for even though a cognition born at the culmination of the excellence of cultivation possesses a vivid appearance, it revolves within the whirlpools of either memory or error, determining an object that is either no more than— or in excess of— the object of a prior experience.
Whence could there be the attainment of the shore of validity?
And how much less, then, its support by way of direct perception?
Or, if it were indeed a case of direct perception, how could there be a transgression of the established rule regarding its object?

Or, if [the Lord] transcends [the senses], how could there be direct perception? Thus, direct perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding one who possesses the sovereignty of universal experience.
Nor is there another means of valid cognition; for that [other means] must be either inference (*anumāna*) or scripture (*āgama*).

Is inference, moreover, that which is "seen through particulars" (*viśeṣato-dṛṣṭa*) or that which is "seen through generalities" (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*)? In this regard, [inference] is not capable of arising with respect to that which is far beyond the entire range of words, because its emergence depends upon the ascertainment of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) preceded by the direct perception of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For those who have never before perceived fire are not able to connect smoke with it as being invariably concomitant.

Furthermore, no inferential mark (*liṅga*), even one based on general observation (*sāmānyato d�ṛṣṭa*), is found that is more effective for directly realizing the creation of all objects than this [argument]:
"Indeed, the world under dispute is dependent upon a single conscious being, because it is not produced by what is insentient, just like one's own healthy body. (YS 4)
Likewise, let the skill in directly manifesting all objects be inferred from the Creator of the world, precisely because the world is an effect. (YŚ 5)

For every effect—such as a jar, a water-pot, a house, and so forth—is understood to be produced by an intelligent agent who perceives the material cause (*upādāna*), the instruments (*upakaraṇa*), the recipient (*sampradāna*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).
And since the subject of dispute, such as the earth, mountains, and great oceans, is also an effect, it too is determined to have an intelligent cause of that same nature.
Nor should it be said that "the quality of being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because that [existence of the whole] is established by reasons such as the arrangement of parts (*avayavasanniveśa*),

and because here everything down to the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)— beginning from other wholes— is understood to be produced by a specific conjunction of various parts that diminishes in sequence, ultimately the four kinds of atoms are the material cause (*upādāna*) of the phenomenal world.

The initial movement of those [elements] has as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) the conjunction of each respective knower of the field (kṣetrajña) with that which is qualified by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) corresponding to it; thus, the instrumental means (upakaraṇa) are the unseen forces characterized as merit and demerit residing in all knowers of the field.

Furthermore, the purpose (prayojana) is the distinction between benefit and harm to conscious beings, consisting of the various types of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) brought about by those [unseen forces].
Those very field-knower (*kṣetrajña*)s who enjoy those [results] are the recipients (*sampradāna*).

Furthermore, these [field-knowers] are not capable of even perceiving their own inherent merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*); therefore, there must exist one distinct from them, skilled in the creation of the entire universe, who possesses a preeminent power of sovereignty consisting of innate, unsurpassed knowledge and consciousness regarding all objects—a conclusion established by the principle of the locus (*adhikaraṇasiddhānta*).
"Why is the preeminent among men (the Creator) not inferred from a mark based on general observation?
To this, the Mīmāṃsakas respond with derision, saying that this is merely the flash of a fickle argument fabricated by one's own mind by someone who does not understand the workings of inference.
For instance, what exactly is intended by this "dependence upon a single conscious agent" in the case of bodies, the world, and so forth?
If it is argued that [the world] is dependent upon Him, what is it that depends on Him? Is it its birth, or its subsistence, or its activity?
In the case of the first two, the example provided is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyahīna*). (YS 6)
Indeed, the body is not produced and maintained by the power of a single conscious being alone.

For those who share in the experience of pleasure and pain dependent upon a particular body, all of them— provided they possess the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) appropriate for that— become the cause of its production and maintenance, just like the possessor of that body himself.

Moreover, the stability of a whole body, characterized by its inherence in its own parts, does not depend on a further conscious agent except through a particular mutual connection of the parts. As for that stability characterized by the vital breath which does depend upon such an agent, it is not possible in the case of the earth and other elements under discussion; thus, we do not observe even a uniform stability that conforms to both the subject and the similar instances.

If, however, [the reason] were "functioning under the dependence of a single consciousness," there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to stones, trees, chariots, and so forth, which are moved by the vigorous and impetuous efforts of many people.
Furthermore, since this is already established by the mere fact of being "begun" (ārabdhatva), this mention of a specific material cause (upādāna-viśeṣa) is redundant for proving this [point].
If one intends to prove merely the state of being dependent on consciousness, then it is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).
For it is produced by us through actions, as an object of enjoyment for conscious experiencers.
And this is logical: that agency is accepted only for those conscious beings who are established for both disputants, because of parsimony (*lāghava*).
Nor can there be a rejection of them on the grounds of their being ignorant of the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth.
The "material cause" refers to earth and the like, while the "means" (*sādhana*) refers to sacrifice, giving, and so forth.
And that all sentient beings whatsoever are capable of realizing it directly.

From this very day, the earth and other elements possess gradual increases and decreases of adventitious properties in their respective parts, rather than undergoing simultaneous and total destruction and origination; thus, the direct perception of the final atom is not conducive to the status of being an agent.
That which is the form of the potency of action, the locus of terms such as *apūrva* (the unseen force), [is what constitutes agency].
Let it not be that [the universal] is perceptible; for it is the possessor of power (the individual) that is the object of the senses.

Indeed, potters and others, when undertaking an effect such as a jar, do not begin that work after having directly perceived the power to produce that effect residing in their materials and instruments, such as clay, the staff, and the wheel.

At most, for those unaware of such a power, the practical engagement with the materials and so forth toward the means of achieving a desired end would be inexplicable; however, in this case, the diverse potencies of karma are understood through scripture.
By those actions, they each fashion their own entire self individually.
Moreover, in this world, only that which is possible to produce and whose materials and so forth are possible to know is observed to have an intelligent agent as its creator.
But such is not the case with the earth, the lords of the earth, the great oceans, and so on; how, then, can they be considered effects?
And how could that [Earth] be within the range of direct perception regarding its material causes, instruments, and so forth?
For only such effects as jars, water-pots, and the like— which are known to be preceded by one who is cognizant of their material causes and so on—
are capable of serving as the basis for inferring a cause possessed of such intelligence.

Furthermore, since an effect such as a jar is understood to have been created by one who is non-omnipotent, possessed of limited power and knowledge, embodied, and one whose desires are not yet fulfilled, a logical reason (*hetu*) that establishes such a creator would be contradictory, as it would prove the opposite of the intended person’s omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth. Nor, this being the case, should one fear the consequence of the total collapse of all inferential practice.

For when an object possessing a mark (liṅgin) falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the very fact of that [other] means of valid cognition obstructs the contrary particulars that would otherwise follow by the force of the mark.

Here, however, when that which is skilled in all emanations— which transcends the functional domain of all other means of valid cognition— is sought to be established, [the inference] presents without distinction even all those properties that possess an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) ascertained through positive and negative pervasion (anvaya-vyatireka).
Moreover,
the actions of a discerning being are pervaded by either self-interest or compassion;
since both are absent in the case of Īśvara, the creation of the world is not tenable.
Because his desires have been fulfilled, he does not create for his own sake;

furthermore, at the time of dissolution, since all instruments of experience such as bodies and sense organs have dissolved, sentient beings are devoid of suffering, and thus there is no impetus from compassion born of seeing those who suffer. Therefore, due to the cessation of both self-interest and compassion—which are the pervading factors—the [creation], which is the pervaded factor, [does not occur].
Even by the activity of a discerning person, [the Lord] must be withdrawn [from such action];

for if He were to create the world solely out of compassion, He would produce a state of constant happiness, and if His actions were to follow [only] that [compassion], His sovereignty would be lost. (12)
Nor is there a rule that agency belongs only to one who has direct perception of the material cause and so forth;

for even a self ignorant of the material cause and the instruments possesses agency with respect to knowledge and other such acts. Therefore, [the reason] is unestablished, contradictory, and subject to the aforementioned fallacy of inconclusiveness.
The world does not possess an agent as previously described, on account of the reason of its being an effect.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the earth, mountains, and so forth do not have [an intelligent] agent as their cause, because they are distinct in nature from well-known effects, like space; or else, because their material causes and instruments are impossible to perceive.
By way of contrast, like a jar or similar objects:
atoms are not perceptible because they are substances of unsurpassed subtlety,
just like jars and the like.
The world is not empty at any time,
because it is time, just like the present time.
The body, the world, and so forth do not have God as their creator, because they are effects, just like that [present time].

"God is not the agent because he lacks a purpose, or because he is bodiless, like the liberated soul. To this we reply: "The fact that [the earth and so forth] are effects cannot be denied in the case of the earth and other such things, because they possess parts, because they possess activity, and because they are qualified by magnitude. (YS 14)
Precisely because of such corporeality, because of being endowed with external perceptibility,
and because of possessing both universals and particulars, [the self is non-eternal], just like a jar and so forth.
We do not observe a specific difference in form restricted to a particular arrangement of parts such that "only this kind of configuration must be produced, and no other"; however,
we do observe that what is possible to produce, and for which the requisite materials and instruments are capable of being known, is indeed produced.
Let that be so;
however, those powers of action and knowledge must be acquired through action and knowledge themselves,

and since these are established in the case of the earth and so forth by the force of the aforementioned proofs, there is no distinction between the body and the world on one hand, and well-known effects such as walls and gate-towers on the other.
Nor is the scope of action limited to this alone; no restriction regarding the object of action has been observed such that we might determine this [world] to be something impossible to produce.

And once its status as an effect is established, a particular person who is skilled in the direct perception of its material cause and so forth, in its supervision, and in its impelling, is indeed established.

And that presiding presence (adhiṣṭhāna) is the proximity of the Lord, who possesses volitions conducive to their activity, just as the individual soul (kṣetrajña) [presides] over its own body and so forth;
and that [proximity], in relation to substances, is characterized by conjunction (saṃyoga).
However, [the relation] consists in a conjunction with those qualities as its nature.
Furthermore, the activity of the atoms is characterized by vibration;
whereas for merit and demerit, it is the state of being accompanied by such auxiliary causes as place, time, and so forth, which are conducive to the arising of their results.
The fruit arises from those very factors of merit and demerit alone,
because all these [other factors], being insentient, are incapable of acting when not presided over by volition.
For indeed, an axe not presided over by a conscious carpenter is not capable of fashioning sacrificial posts and the like, even upon obtaining hundreds of auxiliary conditions such as place and time.

Since seeds, sprouts, and so forth are included within the [very] category [of the subject], the charge of inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra) raised by them is merely due to the ignorance of those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
By this, the charge of inconclusiveness based on pleasure and so forth is also refuted.
Furthermore, it is not appropriate to postulate such a presiding agency for the individual souls (kṣetrajña) merely because they are established for both parties.
Because it is certain that they lack the capacity to perceive subtle, concealed, and other such objects;
for every conceptual construction follows what is observed,
and not what contradicts observation.
Nor is the incapacity of the Lord thus established,
because his existence is proven by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Established by the force of the aforementioned proofs, he is proven to be endowed with the innate power of perceiving all objects and the power of impelling them.
This is because the state of being an effect is invariably concomitant with having been preceded by a capable agent.
As for the objection raised— that this [inference] proves the opposite of the specific qualities [of the creator] by implying limited power, knowledge, and a lack of sovereignty—
that is extremely crude.
Because those [causes] are irrelevant:
for nothing that is being produced requires, for its own production, either the incapacity or the ignorance of the agent directed toward another object;
this is because [the effect] merely implies an agent capable of producing it, and thus the negative-only concomitance (*kevalavyatireka*) is not established.

Since the arising of the effect is accounted for by that much alone, it is illogical to postulate as a cause a non-entity (abhāva) which, being unrelated and performing no function, has as its object something else; furthermore,
one must distinguish whether that ignorance and so forth, which takes all other things as its object, is pervasive (vyāpaka), or whether its scope is limited to only a few objects.
It does not, first of all, have every thing as its object,
because [some things] are not perceived;
for indeed, a potter does not fail to know something other than a jar.
Now, what about [the view that it has] only a few objects?
That too is not [correct], because since its objects are not fixed, one observes its deviation in each particular case. Furthermore, there is nothing established [as such].
That which possesses ignorance and so forth alone experiences agency;
nor must it necessarily be an embodied agent, because the possession of a body is not a conclusive proof [of agency].
Indeed, this self, though distinct from the body, does not simply take up a new body;
for it is impossible for one who lacks yoga to simultaneously assume multiple bodies.

It has been established in the *Ātmacintā* that, upon abandoning the previous body, the self enters another body accompanied by the vital breaths impelled by the karma that brings about the acquisition of a new body.

It is untenable for the Self, which is the agent of the act of presiding over the body, to enter into that very body as its presider; for it is contradictory for a single entity to simultaneously function as both the object and the agent in a single action.

If it is argued that "presiding" (adhiṣṭhāna) is observed to consist in the connection with an effort conducive to the activity of that [body], which exists only for one who possesses a conjunction with a body over which he presides;
[we reply: let it be so, because presiding is impossible for one who is not connected to a single principle (tattva), and therefore there must be a mover who is connected to the object to be moved.
For even other objects being presided over, such as measuring rods and the like, are presided over by means of that which is related to them;
therefore, one should not postulate a separate "connection with the body" beyond the mere connection with the object to be presided over required for the act of presiding.
And it has already been stated that the Lord also possesses a connection with the material causes and instruments of the world.
If it were argued that, regarding an object distinct from one's own body, the capacity to produce a specific activity occurs only by means of the body—
just as it is observed that a potter acts as an initiator toward the staff, wheel, and so forth through the contact of his hands—
that too is not correct.
Since it is observed that by mere intense concentration (*abhidhyāna*) alone, one can expel poison from another's body or cause them to tremble,
[the opponent asks: "How can there be a volition (*saṅkalpa*) consisting of impelling another when no body exists?"
What is it that conceives the body, such that in its absence the body would not exist?
If you say "the instrument" (karaṇa), no; for...
Because the mind is an instrument [of action].
Is the Lord without a mind? Certainly. [Objection:
In that case, would not common attributes such as having a body, merit and demerit, and so forth, necessarily follow?
Not so; for the very strength of the fact that [the world] possesses a capable agent—implied by its being an effect—is sufficient to refute [your position].
Furthermore, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because since the mind is an eternal sense-organ, it is admitted to remain connected even when the body has departed.
For only that which conforms to what is observed and is useful for establishing a pervasion (vyāpti) is admitted;
and [this is not the case] regarding the manifold of the primary elements and their derivatives, whose construction is inconceivable even by the mind of one such as us and whose extent is limitless.

If it is argued that the relationship between "being an effect" and such a creator—as one who possesses a limited body, is a knower of only a few things, whose movement is subject to merit and demerit, and who is thus incapable of creation—has not been observed in the case of jars and the like; [we reply: no. For the Creator is established as one who possesses immeasurable power of knowledge and sovereignty, who is independent of a body and so forth, and who is capable of creating the entire universe through mere volition alone. Thus, the connection between "being an effect" and such a creator is indeed observed in jars and other such things.

Has the connection of smoke with a particular fire been observed in a kitchen or similar place, [a fire] situated on the exceedingly deep slopes of a mountain and associated with a vast, previously unseen mass of fuel,
such that by seeing a particular kind of smoke one might infer a corresponding fire on a mountain peak?

For it is the case that whatever kind of smoke is understood to exist in a certain place, that very kind— capable of producing it— is established by the force of the universal pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) and the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), even if it has not been observed in the instance of the example (*dṛṣṭāntabhūmi*).
Why does this which we are stating not take root in your hearts?

Here too, the state of being an effect—whose necessary connection with a capable agent has been established in the case of jars and the like—is observed in the case of the earth and so forth; thus, it brings to mind an intelligent agent capable of producing it, even though such an agent was never previously seen.

For just as there is a necessary relation of smoke with fire in general— regardless of specific differences such as place, time, or the quantity of fuel— so too is there a determination of a necessary relation of an effect with an intelligent agent in general who is capable of its production, provided that specific attributes such as non-omnipotence, lack of omniscience, corporeality, subjection to merit and demerit, and human nature are excluded; thus, there is no difference between the two cases.

Furthermore, although there is an invariable concomitance between being conjoined with an all-pervading substance and possessing motion on the one hand, and possessing touch on the other, how can the mind— which is conjoined with the self as inferred from the specific qualities of eternal substances such as cognition and pleasure—
be devoid of touch? And how is it that,

while we observe a rule that a substance composed of air (vāyu) which possesses the quality of magnitude has a restricted location for its tangibility, this very rule is reversed in the case of the sense organ of touch?

Even if there were a rule regarding the manifestation of either color or touch in a luminous substance, one must still accept that the eye—which is inferred to be of a luminous nature because it is the means for perceiving color—does not invariably manifest both of those qualities.

Furthermore, although the existence of substances such as the luminous is inferred from the observation of their effects, any specific attributes [of luminosity] are sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible; thus, to accept such attributes would lead to the collapse of many established rules.

Well then, since there is no difference in the sublation by non-perception regarding the specific properties adduced even in the present case, and because it would entail the destruction of the observation of many restrictive rules, such an admission must be made;
thus everything is the same, except for your dogmatic attachment.
For indeed, such policies are observed.
Just as the subject of dispute, such as atoms and so forth, acts as impelled by an intelligent being,
because it is insentient; for whatever is insentient acts in that manner.
Just like such things as a ball;
likewise, the external and internal activities under discussion are preceded by material causes, instruments, and perception, because they are effects, exactly like those [examples].
That [perception] is perceptible because it is an object of knowledge and because it is a category of existence, like a jar and so forth.
This [body] follows the will of another because it lacks consciousness, like one's own body.

All sentient beings perform their functions when presided over by a single [consciousness], because they act as agents in dependence upon a connection with a body, just like the sense of touch and the other [faculties]. (YS 17)
The world, which is the subject of dispute, has a single primary Puruṣa as its cause,
because it consists of both sentient and insentient entities, just like the territory of a single king.
